content: Ipratropium bromide, administered via inhalation, is an anticholinergic agent approved by the FDA for the treatment of bronchospasm associated with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), including chronic bronchitis and emphysema. It works by inhibiting vagally mediated reflexes through antagonism of acetylcholine, a neurotransmitter released from the vagus nerve. This prevents increases in intracellular cyclic guanosine monophosphate (cyclic GMP) levels, which are caused by the interaction of acetylcholine with muscarinic receptors on bronchial smooth muscle. The usual adult dosage of ipratropium bromide inhalation solution is 500 mcg (one unit-dose vial) administered three to four times daily via oral nebulization, with doses spaced 6 to 8 hours apart. The solution can be mixed with albuterol or metaproterenol in the nebulizer if used within one hour. However, the stability and safety of mixing ipratropium bromide with other drugs in a nebulizer have not been established. Common adverse reactions include headache, dizziness, nervousness, back pain, chest pain, dry mouth, nausea, coughing, dyspnea, bronchitis, and upper respiratory tract infections. Less common adverse effects include tachycardia, palpitations, eye pain, urinary retention, urinary tract infections, and urticaria. Rare cases of hypersensitivity reactions, such as urticaria, angioedema, rash, bronchospasm, and oropharyngeal edema, have been reported. Patients with a history of allergies to other drugs or foods may be at higher risk for these reactions. Ipratropium bromide is contraindicated in patients with known or suspected hypersensitivity to ipratropium bromide, atropine, or its derivatives. It should be used with caution in patients with narrow-angle glaucoma, prostatic hypertrophy, or bladder-neck obstruction. Direct contact of the solution with the eyes should be avoided, as it may cause temporary blurred vision, precipitation or worsening of narrow-angle glaucoma, or eye pain. The use of ipratropium bromide as a single agent for the relief of bronchospasm in acute COPD exacerbations has not been adequately studied. Drugs with a faster onset of action may be preferable as initial therapy in such situations. Combination therapy with ipratropium bromide and beta-agonists has not been shown to be more effective than either drug alone in reversing bronchospasm associated with acute COPD exacerbations. In clinical trials, significant improvements in pulmonary function (e.g., FEV1 increases of 15% or more) were observed within 15 to 30 minutes of administration, peaking at 1 to 2 hours, and persisting for 4 to 5 hours in most patients. However, ipratropium bromide did not consistently improve subjective symptom scores or quality of life measures over a 12-week study period. The safety and effectiveness of ipratropium bromide in pediatric patients under the age of 12 have not been established. There is no FDA guidance on its use in geriatric populations, specific gender or racial groups, or patients with renal or hepatic impairment. It should be used during pregnancy only if clearly needed, as adequate studies in pregnant women are lacking. It is not known whether ipratropium bromide is excreted in human milk, but caution is advised when administering it to nursing mothers. Ipratropium bromide is minimally absorbed systemically after inhalation, and much of the administered dose is swallowed but not absorbed. It is partially metabolized and does not penetrate the blood-brain barrier. In animal studies, it has shown no evidence of teratogenic effects or carcinogenic potential at tested doses. However, at high doses, it has been associated with increased resorption and decreased conception rates in rats. Patients should be counseled to use ipratropium bromide inhalation solution consistently as prescribed and to avoid alcohol interactions, as the effects of alcohol with this medication have not been established. The solution should be stored between 59°F (15°C) and 86°F (30°C), protected from light, and unused vials should remain in their foil pouch.
